newsitem.title: SWEDEN: CHAMPAGNE STILL SWEET AFTER 80 YEARS UNDER WATER.
newsitem.headline: CHAMPAGNE STILL SWEET AFTER 80 YEARS UNDER WATER.

text.p: Divers have sampled a bottle of 90-year-old champagne brought up from the wreckage of a ship carrying luxury goods to pre-revolutionary Russia and pronounced it thoroughly drinkable.
Thousands of bottles of champagne, cognac and fine wine have been found in the wreckage of the Swedish ketch Jonkoping, which was torpedoed in the Baltic Sea south of Finland in 1916 by a submarine.

The head of the consortium diving to inspect the wreckage, Claes Bergvall, described the sensation of drinking the 90-year-old French champagne -- the label was lost but the cork revealed a 1907 vintage -- as "dizzying."
"All I can say is that the champagne tasted exquisite," he added.
The unusual wine tasting took place at dawn on Monday after the consortium ended the reconnoitring phase of its dive, which confirmed suspicions that the wreckage was packed with vintage goodies.

"It was an improbable sensation. We didn't really think you could take a bottle up from that wreckage and that it would be ok. We thought it would explode or break but there was no problem," said Bergvall.

The 25-metre (80-foot) long Jonkoping was sunk in 1916, during World War One, by a German submarine south of Finland and has lain in 60 metres (200 feet) of water since then. The slightly salty Baltic waters are well-known to act as preservatives of many substances.
The Jonkoping left the Swedish port of Gavle on October 28, 1916 after a storm that had lasted a week, bound for Finland and Petrograd (now St. Petersburg).
The submarine, U-Boat 22, had a field day after the storm, sinking six other ships. Sweden was neutral during the war.
The wreck was found in June and Bergvall and his team have now halted work while they seek sponsorship to raise the cargo, which he says could be worth up to 500 million crowns.
The ship's cargo consists of 35,000 litres of cognac, 5,000 bottles of champagne and almost 6,000 litres of wine.
The cognac and champagne, presumably of the finest quality, were destined for the officer corps of the Tsar's imperial army. The wine had been ordered by the central bank of Finland.

Wine experts say the quality of the bottles that have been discovered remains an unknown. The drinks may have fared better under the sea -- in cool, dark conditions that could resemble the caves where champagne is stored.
The biggest danger would be seepage of water into the bottles, they added.
Bergvall said he hoped to dive again with two weeks to bring up loose bottles scattered around the wreckage, after which bottles could be unloaded by the crate.
